items.title: Rebuilding a manufacturer's global website
items.summary: Re-architected a manufacturer's brand site and multi-language presence, cutting first contentful paint to under 1.5 seconds.

detail.overview: One rebuild turned the website from a business card into a lead channel.
background: The legacy site ran on a decade-old template with tangled navigation and a poor mobile experience; overseas buyers needed more than three steps to reach specs and contact details.
Content updates went through an external agency, so a single product change took a week — the marketing team could not self-serve.
approach: We co-created the information architecture with sales and marketing, collapsing content into a three-level products → models → specs structure and defining a configurable multi-language content model.
The front end statically renders with Next.js, with image and font strategies to keep the critical path minimal, while structured data and a sitemap cover SEO.

steps.title: Research & information architecture
steps.text: Interviewed 8 internal users and 5 overseas buyers; delivered a sitemap and content inventory.

steps.title: Visual & component design
steps.text: Built design tokens and 20+ components on the brand palette, delivered high-fidelity screens.

steps.title: Build & content migration
steps.text: Three languages developed in parallel with scripts to migrate and proof historical material.

steps.title: Launch & handover
steps.text: Connected analytics and indexing, trained the marketing team to maintain content.

items.title: SaaS console and billing system
items.summary: A multi-tenant console covering subscriptions, usage billing and support tickets — the full loop from trial to paying customer.

detail.overview: Subscriptions, usage and tickets in one account model so commercialisation can move.
background: The product only had a trial build: no accounts, plan management or billing — every contract was handled offline with manual reconciliation.
Operations needed to configure plans and discounts themselves without waiting for development.
approach: We designed a four-layer model of tenants, members, subscriptions and usage, persisting billing events and aligning them with payment callbacks so every invoice is traceable.
The console mixes server rendering with targeted client interactivity, keeping first paint of key list pages under a second.

steps.title: Commercial flow mapping
steps.text: Turned trial, conversion, renewal and refund into an explicit state machine.

steps.title: Data model & APIs
steps.text: Defined tenant/subscription/usage models with idempotent billing endpoints.

steps.title: Console & billing
steps.text: Shipped plan configuration, usage dashboards, invoices and self-service receipts.

steps.title: Integration & load testing
steps.text: Reconciled payment callbacks and load-tested concurrency.

items.title: Cross-border e-commerce store
items.summary: Built a standalone store and operations back office from scratch, wiring payments, inventory and shipping — GMV passed 10M in three months.

detail.overview: Shipping both 'can sell' and 'can operate' in a single build.
background: The brand planned to start on a hosted site builder, but multi-currency display, tax rules and integration with their own marketing stack kept hitting limits.
They needed something that launches fast yet leaves room for custom logic.
approach: A headless architecture: a statically generated storefront for speed, catalogue and content served from the CMS, with payments and inventory behind dedicated APIs.
The operations back office exposes banners, promo codes and stock alerts so marketers can prepare a campaign without developers.

steps.title: Selection & architecture
steps.text: Compared site builders vs custom build with a cost and extensibility analysis.

steps.title: Transaction chain
steps.text: Built cart, promotions, payment, tax calculation and shipping lookup end to end.

steps.title: Operations back office
steps.text: Delivered banners, promo codes, inventory and order management.

steps.title: Peak readiness
steps.text: Load testing, cache tuning and an on-call plus rollback plan for launch day.

items.title: Online learning platform
items.summary: Courses, assignments, live sessions and learning data in one platform — halving the admin team's daily workload.

detail.overview: Scheduling, assignments and learning data on a single spine — no more spreadsheet shuffling.
background: The academy managed courses and homework with spreadsheets and group chats; staff spent hours every week reconciling rosters and progress.
Learners lacked a continuous path, and completion rates had stagnated.
approach: We modelled courses, cohorts, assignments and live sessions into one scheduling core so most admin tasks happen in a single screen.
The learner experience puts the next step front and centre, with reminders that keep momentum going.

steps.title: Shadowing & interviews
steps.text: Followed the admin team for a full week to locate delays and error hotspots.

steps.title: Scheduling & permissions
steps.text: Designed the cohort/course/instructor permission matrix with conflict checks.

steps.title: Learner experience
steps.text: Rebuilt learning paths, assignment submission and replay playback.

steps.title: Data dashboards
steps.text: Shipped completion, engagement and admin-efficiency dashboards.

items.title: Internal operations portal
items.summary: Moved approval flows scattered across spreadsheets and email into one system with tickets, permissions and audit trails.

detail.overview: Map the process first, systemise second: approvals consolidated in one place.
background: Over 20 approval flows were spread across emails and paper signatures, often stalling at 'who do I ask next?'.
Without an audit trail, accountability after the fact was impossible.
approach: We inventoried and simplified the flows — removing 40% of redundant steps — then implemented them on a configurable workflow engine so new flows need no code changes.
RBAC permissions and full audit logging were added to satisfy internal controls.

steps.title: Process inventory
steps.text: Mapped 20+ flows and cut 40% of redundant steps.

steps.title: Workflow engine
steps.text: Configurable nodes, conditions and cc rules.

steps.title: Permissions & audit
steps.text: Permission matrix plus complete operation logs.

steps.title: Rollout & maintenance
steps.text: Department-by-department training, then monthly iteration.

items.title: Business analytics dashboard
items.summary: A real-time executive dashboard unifying metrics from scattered systems on a single definition, refreshed daily.

detail.overview: One metric definition so the daily business review stops arguing about numbers.
background: Each business system defined metrics differently, so the same figure disagreed across reports and meetings started with a debate.
Monthly reports took the data team three days of manual assembly.
approach: We co-authored a metric dictionary with the client, enforcing definitions in the ETL and API layers so the front end only consumes a single source of truth.
Dashboards are role-based: executives see the overview, operators see detail, with drill-down and export.

steps.title: Metric alignment
steps.text: Confirmed 120+ metric definitions with business owners and published a dictionary.

steps.title: Data pipeline
steps.text: Scheduled jobs with validation and alerting on anomalies.

steps.title: Dashboard build
steps.text: Overview, detail and drill-down views per role.

steps.title: Ongoing operations
steps.text: Monthly metric iterations with stable job reliability.

contact.title: Ready to start your project?
contact.subtitle: Send your requirements and we will reply within one business day with an initial scope and budget range.

faq.q: How long does a website project take?
faq.a: A typical corporate site takes 3–6 weeks; with multiple languages and content migration, 6–8 weeks. You receive a milestone schedule right after discovery.
Fixed price per project or time-and-materials, with monthly subscriptions for maintenance. Scope is agreed up front so there are no surprises mid-project.

faq.q: Can you take on just part of the work?
faq.a: Yes. Common splits are design first, or a single module first — we quote by module and continue from there.

faq.q: Do you support us after launch?
faq.a: Yes. Delivery includes training and documentation, and you can move to a monthly maintenance subscription covering incidents, security patches and small iterations.

cta.title: Have a project in mind?
cta.text: Whether it is a 0-to-1 product or a legacy system that needs rescuing, let's talk it through before you decide.
